definition: A message authentication code built by running a message and a secret key through a hash function. A receiver holding the same key recomputes it, and a match proves the message was not altered and came from someone who knows the key.
example: An API signs each request with HMAC-SHA-256 using a key shared with the client; the server recomputes the value and rejects any request where it differs.
keyPoints: Gives integrity and authenticity, not confidentiality
Both sides share one secret key (symmetric)
No non-repudiation: either key holder could have made the tag, unlike a digital signature made with a private key
A plain hash proves integrity only, since anyone can recompute it; HMAC adds the key
Works with any approved hash, for example HMAC-SHA-256
CompTIA's acronym list expands HMAC as hashed message authentication code; same thing

definition: A property of a key exchange in which every session gets fresh keys from a new, short-lived (ephemeral) Diffie-Hellman exchange, so stealing a long-term key later cannot unlock sessions recorded earlier. DHE is ephemeral Diffie-Hellman; ECDHE is the elliptic curve version.
example: An attacker records months of TLS traffic and later steals the server's private key, but cannot decrypt the recordings because each session used its own ECDHE key that was thrown away.
keyPoints: The E in DHE and ECDHE means ephemeral: a new key pair per session, then discarded
The server's long-term key only signs the exchange; it never protects the session key itself
Static RSA key exchange has no forward secrecy: one stolen key decrypts every recorded session
TLS 1.3 removed static RSA and static Diffie-Hellman, so all its public-key key exchanges give forward secrecy; resuming with a pre-shared key alone, without a fresh (EC)DHE, does not
IPsec offers PFS as an option: a new Diffie-Hellman exchange for each security association

definition: A certificate whose Subject Alternative Name extension lists several identities it is valid for, such as specific DNS names, IP addresses or email addresses, so one certificate can cover many named hosts.
example: One certificate lists example.com, www.example.com and shop.example.net in its SAN field and secures all three sites.
keyPoints: Names each covered host exactly, even across different domains
Wildcard (*.example.com) covers any single-level subdomain of one domain but not the bare domain; a SAN entry can add it
Browsers match the name you visit against the SAN entries
The CA must verify every name in the SAN before signing
Adding a name means reissuing the certificate

definition: An optional PKI component that checks the identity of people or devices asking for certificates and passes approved requests to the certificate authority, which then issues and signs the certificate.
example: A company's help desk acts as the RA: it confirms an employee's badge and HR record, then forwards the request so the internal CA can issue the user's certificate.
keyPoints: RA verifies identity; CA signs and issues
An RA never signs certificates
Takes administrative work off the CA
Can be a person, a team or software
Trap: the entity that signs a certificate is always the CA, never the RA

definition: A starting value fed into a cipher alongside the key so that encrypting the same data twice with the same key gives different ciphertext. It does not need to be secret, but in many modes it must never repeat with the same key.
example: AES-GCM normally uses a 96-bit IV, a new one for every message. If a device reused an IV with the same key, an attacker could work out the authentication key from the two messages and forge new ones.
keyPoints: Adds randomness so identical plaintexts do not produce identical ciphertexts
Sent in the clear with the ciphertext; it is not a key
Reuse with the same key can break confidentiality and, in GCM, authentication
In GCM and CTR it is often called a nonce (number used once)
CBC needs more than uniqueness: its IV must be unpredictable, for example random
